writer: claude-opus-5-5 (written by hand in Claude Code)
summary: Siblings play a unique role in each other's lives. The bond mixes parent-like companionship with friend-like influence. It is usually more equal than ties across generations. Siblings often spend more childhood time together than with parents. The relationship is often the longest-lasting in a person's life. In industrialized cultures, sibling ties are usually optional. In nonindustrialized cultures, close ties are often obligatory. The bond is fairly stable from infancy to middle childhood. A responsive older sibling can become a source of comfort. Adolescence often brings more conflict and emotional distance. Intimacy usually rises again in young adulthood. Siblings can influence each other much as peers do. Positive sibling relationships support healthy development. Conflict and aggression can promote delinquency. Adult siblings often keep in touch. Sisters stay in contact most, and brothers least. Living close by increases contact. Divorce, widowhood or a family death usually brings siblings closer. Sibling rivalry often stems from competing for parents' attention. Psychologist Sylvia Rimm says it is most intense between siblings close in age and of the same gender. Freud linked sibling rivalry to the Oedipus complex, a view now largely discredited.
